questions.title: Network
questions.text: Define the term **computer network** and give **one** reason why a school uses one.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Two or more devices connected to communicate / share data (1)
- reason: share printers / files / Internet; central backup; log on anywhere; communication (1)
scheme.model_answer: Two or more computers connected so they can communicate and share resources; the school can share one printer and Internet connection between all PCs.

questions.title: LAN or WAN
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each statement describes a LAN or a WAN.

prefill: Covers a small geographical area such as one building
Often uses communication links rented from telecom companies
Usually has a higher data transfer rate
The Internet is an example
Usually owned by a single organisation

scheme.mark_scheme: LAN; WAN; LAN; WAN; LAN (1 each)

questions.title: Compare LAN and WAN
questions.text: Compare **two** features of a LAN and a WAN.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two comparative points mentioning both (1 each): area small vs large; owned by one organisation vs rented links; faster vs slower; fewer vs more errors; cheap vs expensive; cable / Wi-Fi vs fibre / satellite
scheme.model_answer: 1 A LAN covers a small area like a school, whereas a WAN covers a large area like a country. 2 A LAN is owned by one organisation, whereas a WAN uses links rented from telecom companies.

questions.title: Network size
questions.text: A student connects wireless earbuds and a smartwatch to their phone by Bluetooth. What type of network is this?

scheme.mark_scheme: A

questions.title: Intranet
questions.text: Define the term **intranet**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A private network of one organisation (1)
- using Internet technologies (web pages, browsers, TCP/IP), accessible only to authorised users (1)
scheme.model_answer: A private network inside an organisation that uses web pages and Internet protocols but can only be used by its authorised members.

questions.title: Internet or intranet
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each feature belongs to the Internet or an intranet.

prefill: Can be accessed by anyone with a connection
Contains a school's internal timetables and policies
Information is controlled by one organisation
A global network of interconnected networks

scheme.mark_scheme: Internet; intranet; intranet; Internet (1 each)

questions.title: Extranet
questions.text: An extranet allows selected people outside an organisation, such as parents or suppliers, to log in to part of its intranet.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: Client-server or P2P
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show which network model each statement describes.

prefill: Backups are made centrally
Every computer has equal status
Cheaper and easier to set up
User accounts and permissions are managed in one place

scheme.mark_scheme: CS; P2P; P2P; CS (1 each)

questions.title: School network model
questions.text: Explain why a school with 400 computers should use a client-server network rather than a peer-to-peer network.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): central security — accounts / permissions / antivirus; central automatic backup; students can log on from any computer and see their files; easier to manage / install software for many PCs; performs better with many users
scheme.model_answer: The server controls user accounts and permissions, so security is managed centrally; all files are backed up automatically on the server; and students can log in from any of the 400 computers and reach their own files.

questions.title: Peer-to-peer drawback
questions.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of a peer-to-peer network.

scheme.mark_scheme: Disadvantage (1) + explanation (1): no central backup — files on each PC can be lost; weak security — each user controls own PC; a switched-off peer cannot share files; slower with many users
scheme.model_answer: There is no central backup, so if one computer fails, the files stored only on it are lost.

questions.title: Transmission media
questions.text: Match each transmission medium to its description.

right.text: Copper wires carrying electrical signals, up to about 100 m
Pulses of light; very fast over long distances
Radio waves for a wireless LAN
Short-range radio for a personal area network

questions.title: Wired vs wireless
questions.text: A café wants customers to connect their laptops and phones. Give **two** advantages and **two** disadvantages of a wireless connection compared with a wired one.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantages (1 each): mobility / customers can sit anywhere; phones and tablets can connect; no cables to install / cheaper / no trip hazard; easy to add many devices. Disadvantages (1 each): slower / speed varies; interference; signals can be intercepted — less secure; limited range
scheme.model_answer: Advantages: customers can connect from any seat; phones without network ports can connect. Disadvantages: the signals can be intercepted, so it is less secure; speed drops with many users and interference.

questions.title: Fibre-optic
questions.text: Explain why fibre-optic cable is used to connect two school buildings 800 m apart.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Copper twisted pair only works up to about 100 m; fibre carries signals over long distances (1)
- very high speed / no electrical interference / secure (1)
scheme.model_answer: Copper Ethernet only reaches about 100 m, but fibre carries light signals for kilometres at very high speed without electrical interference.

questions.title: Topologies
questions.text: Match each topology to its description.

right.text: All devices share one backbone cable with terminators
Each device connects to two others in a loop
Each device has its own cable to a central switch
Devices connect to many or all other devices
A combination of two or more topologies

scheme.mark_scheme: Bus–R1, Ring–R2, Star–R3, Mesh–R4, Mixed–R5.

questions.title: Features of topologies
questions.text: Tick (✓) the **one** topology each statement best describes.

prefill: If the central device fails, the whole network stops
Uses the least cable
Data can take many different routes
Data travels in one direction, passing each device
Has terminators at each end of the main cable

scheme.mark_scheme: Star; bus; mesh; ring; bus (1 each)

questions.title: Star and bus
questions.text: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of each topology.

scheme.mark_scheme: Star adv: one cable failure affects only one device / easy to add devices / no collisions with switch / easy to find faults (1). Star dis: switch is a single point of failure / more cable / cost of switch (1). Bus adv: cheap / least cable / easy to add (1). Bus dis: backbone failure stops all / collisions / slow with many devices / hard to find faults (1)
scheme.model_answer: Star: if one cable breaks, only that computer is affected; but if the switch fails, everything stops. Bus: cheap because it needs little cable; but a break in the backbone stops the whole network.

questions.title: Mesh for a bank
questions.text: Explain why a bank connects its data centres in a mesh topology even though it is expensive.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Many routes between data centres / no single point of failure (1)
- if one link fails data is rerouted, so the bank's services keep working / transactions are not lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: In a mesh there are many routes, so if one link fails, data is sent another way and the bank's systems keep running without interruption.

questions.title: A school with two buildings
questions.text: A school has a computer room in each of its two buildings. In each room every PC is connected to a switch, and the two switches are connected by a fibre-optic cable.

parts.title: Topology
parts.text: Identify the overall topology of the school network.

scheme.mark_scheme: Mixed / hybrid (stars joined together; accept extended star / tree) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Mixed (hybrid) topology

parts.title: Advantage
parts.text: Explain **one** advantage of connecting the PCs in each room to a switch.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage (1) + explanation (1): one broken cable affects only one PC, others keep working; easy to add PCs by plugging into the switch; switch sends data only to the destination → fast / secure
scheme.model_answer: Each PC has its own cable, so if one cable is damaged only that PC loses its connection and the rest of the room keeps working.

parts.title: Risk
parts.text: Explain what happens if the fibre-optic cable between the buildings is cut.

scheme.mark_scheme: PCs in each room still communicate with each other through their switch (1); but the two rooms / buildings cannot communicate, e.g. cannot reach a server in the other building (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each room still works as its own star network, but the two buildings can no longer exchange data, so one building may lose access to the server or the Internet.

questions.title: Types of network
questions.text: An education company has an office in Astana with 60 computers and branches in five other cities.

parts.title: LAN vs WAN
parts.text: The Astana office uses a LAN and the branches are linked by a WAN. Compare LAN and WAN in terms of:

scheme.mark_scheme: Each comparison mentioning both (1 each): LAN small area / one building vs WAN large area / several cities; LAN owned by the company vs WAN uses links rented from telecom providers; LAN faster vs WAN slower / more latency; LAN cheap vs WAN expensive
scheme.model_answer: Area: the LAN covers one office, whereas the WAN covers several cities. Ownership: the company owns the LAN, whereas the WAN uses lines rented from telecom companies. Speed: the LAN is faster than the WAN. Cost: the LAN is cheap, whereas the WAN is expensive to rent.

parts.title: Intranet
parts.text: The company publishes staff timetables and policies on an intranet rather than on the Internet. Explain **three** reasons for this.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): private — only staff with logins can see; more secure / behind firewall; information controlled / reliable / up to date; internal information not visible to the public / competitors; faster access inside the network
scheme.model_answer: Only staff with a login can see the information, so it stays private; it is protected by the company firewall; and the company controls the content, so it is reliable and up to date.

parts.title: Network model
parts.text: Explain why the office should use a client-server network instead of peer-to-peer.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): central security / user accounts; central backup; files in one place / log on anywhere; easier management of 60 PCs / software updates; better performance for many users
scheme.model_answer: The server manages user accounts and permissions centrally, backs up all files automatically, and lets staff log in from any of the 60 computers to reach their files.

questions.title: Connections
questions.text: The office must decide how to connect its computers, printers and staff laptops.

parts.title: Wired vs wireless
parts.text: Tick (✓) whether each statement applies to a wired or a wireless connection.

prefill: Users can move around the building while connected
Signals are harder to intercept
Speed is affected by walls and distance
Usually gives a faster and more stable connection

scheme.mark_scheme: Wireless; wired; wireless; wired (1 each)

parts.title: Recommendation
parts.text: The server room and desktop PCs use cable; staff laptops use Wi-Fi. Evaluate this decision.

scheme.mark_scheme: Up to 4 (1 each): wired for server / desktops — fast, stable, secure for heavy data; desktops do not move so mobility not needed; Wi-Fi for laptops — mobility / meetings anywhere / no extra cables; drawback: Wi-Fi less secure → needs WPA2/WPA3 / strong password; drawback: Wi-Fi slower with many users; conclusion: sensible combination
scheme.model_answer: Cabling the server and desktops is sensible: they don't move and need fast, stable, secure connections. Wi-Fi suits laptops because staff move between rooms. However, Wi-Fi can be intercepted, so WPA3 encryption is needed, and it may slow down with many users. Overall it is a good balance.

questions.title: Topologies
questions.text: The network manager compares four topologies: **bus**, **ring**, **star** and **mesh**.

parts.title: Describe
parts.text: Describe how the devices are connected in each topology.

scheme.mark_scheme: Bus: all on one backbone cable with terminators (1). Ring: each device connected to two others in a loop (1). Star: each device has its own link to a central switch / hub (1). Mesh: each device connected to several / all others (1)
scheme.model_answer: Bus: every device joins one main cable. Ring: devices form a closed loop, each linked to two neighbours. Star: each device is cabled to a central switch. Mesh: devices are linked to many or all other devices.

parts.title: Ring
parts.text: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of a ring topology.

scheme.mark_scheme: Advantage: no collisions / equal access / good under heavy load (1). Disadvantage: one failed link or device stops the network / adding devices disrupts it / data passes through other devices (1)
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: no data collisions because only one device sends at a time. Disadvantage: if one link breaks, the whole ring stops.

parts.title: Recommend
parts.text: Recommend a topology for the office of 60 computers and justify your choice by comparing it with **one** other topology.

scheme.mark_scheme: Recommend star (or justified alternative) (1); justification points (up to 3): one cable failure affects only one PC whereas bus backbone failure stops all; easy to add PCs; no collisions with switch / faster than bus with 60 PCs; cheaper and simpler than mesh; drawback acknowledged — switch single point of failure
scheme.model_answer: Star. Each PC has its own cable to a switch, so a broken cable affects only one PC, whereas in a bus a break in the backbone stops all 60 PCs. A switch sends data only to the destination, so there are no collisions, and new PCs are easy to add. It is also much cheaper than a mesh.

parts.title: Mesh
parts.text: Explain why the Internet is described as a mesh of networks.

scheme.mark_scheme: Routers / networks are connected to many others (1); so there are many possible routes and data can be rerouted if a link fails (1)
scheme.model_answer: Its routers are linked to many other routers, so there are many paths between any two points and data can go another way if one link fails.

summary: What a computer network is and why networks are used, LAN, WAN and other network sizes, the Internet, intranets and extranets, client-server and peer-to-peer models, wired and wireless transmission media, and the advantages and disadvantages of bus, ring, star, mesh and mixed topologies.

blocks.content: Two or more computers or devices **connected together** so that they can **communicate** and **share resources** — data, files, printers, software and an Internet connection.

items.title: Advantages of networking
items.content:
- **Share resources** — one printer, scanner or Internet connection for many users.
- **Share files and data** — work on the same documents; central databases.
- **Communication** — e-mail, messaging, video calls.
- **Central management** — software installed, updated and backed up from one place.
- **Users can log on from any computer** and see their own files.

items.title: Disadvantages of networking
items.content:
- **Cost** of cables, switches, servers and a network manager.
- **Security risks** — viruses and hackers can spread through the network.
- If a **server or key device fails**, many users are affected.
- Needs specialist **maintenance**; the network can become **slow** with heavy traffic.

blocks.content: Any device connected to a network that can send or receive data — a computer, printer, phone, server, switch or router.

blocks.title: LAN vs WAN
rows: **Small**: one building or site (school, office, home)
Usually owned and managed by **one organisation**
Uses infrastructure **rented** from telecom companies (leased lines, satellites)
Fibre-optic cables, telephone lines, satellite, microwave
The **Internet**; a bank linking all its branches across Kazakhstan

blocks.title: Other network sizes
rows: A few metres around one person
Phone + wireless earbuds + smartwatch by Bluetooth
A city-wide network of libraries or CCTV

blocks.content: "Compare" needs a point that mentions **both** sides: "A LAN covers a **small geographical area** such as one building, **whereas** a WAN covers a **large area** such as several countries."

A **global public network of interconnected networks** (a WAN) that communicate using the **TCP/IP** protocols. Services that run on it include the **World Wide Web**, e-mail, file transfer, online games and video calls.

A **private network** belonging to **one organisation**, which uses **Internet technologies** (web pages, browsers, TCP/IP) but can only be accessed by **authorised members** — for example a school portal with timetables and homework.

blocks.title: Internet vs intranet
rows: **Private** — only employees / students with a login, often only inside the organisation
Public information from millions of sources
**Internal** information: timetables, policies, forms, news, staff directory
Lower — content and users not controlled
Controlled by the organisation, usually reliable and up to date

blocks.title: Extranet
blocks.content: Part of an intranet made available to **selected outsiders** — for example parents, suppliers or partner schools — through a **secure login**. Parents checking marks in an e-journal use an extranet.

items.title: Client-server
items.content:
- One or more powerful **servers** provide **services** — files, e-mail, web pages, printing, logins, databases.
- **Clients** (users' computers) **request** these services.
- Management, **security** and **backup** are **central**.

items.title: Peer-to-peer (P2P)
items.content:
- All computers are **equal** (peers): each can share its own files and resources and use those of others.
- There is **no central server**; each peer is both client and server.

blocks.content:
flowchart TB
  S[Server: files, logins, backup]
  C1[Client 1] -- request --> S
  C2[Client 2] -- request --> S
  C3[Client 3] -- request --> S
  S -. response .-> C1
  S -. response .-> C2
  S -. response .-> C3
blocks.caption: Client-server: clients send requests, the server sends responses

blocks.title: Client-server vs peer-to-peer
rows: **Central** — accounts, permissions and antivirus managed on the server
Each user manages their own computer; **weaker** security
Each computer separately — data can be lost
No single point of failure, but a peer that is switched off cannot share its files
Slows down as more users share resources
Homes, small offices, file sharing (torrents), some video calls

blocks.title: Wired transmission media
rows: Electrical signals in pairs of twisted wires
Cheap, common in LANs, up to 100 m, 1–10 Gbit/s
Copper core with a metal shield
Better shielding; cable TV / old networks
**Very fast**, very long distances (km), no electrical interference, hard to tap; more expensive

blocks.title: Wireless transmission
rows: Wireless LANs at home, school, cafés
Phones and tablets on the move

blocks.title: Wired vs wireless
rows: **Interference** from walls, microwaves and other networks
Signals can be **intercepted** from outside — needs encryption (**WPA2/WPA3**) and strong passwords
Users **move freely**; phones and tablets connect
Cables are costly to lay and hard to move; **trip hazard**
**Easy** to add devices, no cables; cheaper in old buildings
Up to ~100 m per copper cable (fibre much more)
Limited by router range; needs extra access points
Many devices, but each gets less bandwidth

blocks.content: The **layout** of a network — how its **nodes** are **connected** to each other and how data travels between them.

blocks.title: The basic topologies

items.title: Bus
items.content:
- All devices are connected to **one main cable (backbone)** with a **terminator** at each end.
- Data is sent along the backbone and **every** device receives it; only the addressed device keeps it.
- Two devices sending at once cause a **collision**.

items.title: Ring
items.content:
- Each device is connected to **exactly two others**, forming a **loop**.
- Data travels **in one direction**, passing through each device until it reaches the destination (often using a **token** that gives permission to send).

items.title: Star
items.content:
- Every device has its **own cable** to a **central switch** (or hub).
- The switch sends data **only to the destination** device.
- The most common topology for school and home LANs.

items.title: Mesh
items.content:
- Devices are connected to **many** (partial mesh) or **all** (full mesh) other devices.
- Data can take **several routes**; if one link fails, another is used.
- The **Internet** is a partial mesh of routers.

items.title: Mixed (hybrid)
items.content: - A combination of two or more topologies — e.g. several **star** networks in different classrooms joined by a **bus** or **mesh** backbone.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages
rows: **Cheap** — needs the least cable; easy to add a device; no central device needed
If the **backbone fails**, the whole network stops; **collisions** → slow with many devices; hard to find faults; low security (all devices see the data)
**No collisions** — one device sends at a time; performs well under heavy load; **equal (fair) access** for every device
One broken link or device can **stop the whole network**; adding or removing a device **disrupts** the network; data passes through other devices
A failed cable or device affects **only that device**; **easy to add** devices; fast and secure with a **switch** (no collisions); easy to find faults
**Central switch** is a **single point of failure**; needs **more cable** than bus; the switch costs money
**Very reliable** — many routes, no single point of failure; can carry a lot of traffic; data can be rerouted
**Expensive** — many cables / links; **complex** to set up and manage; much redundant cabling
Flexible — combines the strengths of each part; easy to **expand**
Complex to design and manage; a failure in the backbone affects several parts

blocks.title: Choosing a topology
blocks.content:
- A **small school computer room** of 30 PCs → **star**: if one cable breaks only one PC is affected, and new PCs are easy to add.
- A **bank's data centres** that must never go offline → **mesh**: many routes, so one failed link does not stop transactions.
- A **school with several buildings** → **mixed**: a star in each building, connected by a fibre backbone.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Compare a LAN and a WAN. [2]**
A LAN covers a **small area** such as a school, **whereas** a WAN covers a **large area** such as a country (1). A LAN is usually **owned** by one organisation, **whereas** a WAN uses **rented** telecom links (1).

**Q: Give two differences between an intranet and the Internet. [2]**
An intranet is **private** to one organisation and needs a **login**, whereas the Internet is **public** (1); intranet content is **controlled** by the organisation, whereas Internet content comes from anyone (1).

**Q: Give one advantage of a star topology and one disadvantage of a bus topology. [2]**
Star: if one cable fails, **only that device** is affected (1). Bus: if the **backbone** fails, the **whole network** stops (1).

**Q: Explain why a school uses a client-server network rather than peer-to-peer. [2]**
Security and backup are **managed centrally** on the server (1), so student files are backed up automatically and access can be controlled with **user accounts** (1).

- Saying a LAN is "small" and a WAN is "big" without saying **area**.
- Confusing the **Internet** (the network) with the **World Wide Web** (web pages that use it).
- Saying star "has no single point of failure" — the **switch** is one.
- Writing an advantage that is only the opposite of a disadvantage you already gave.
